{{Short description|Computer-assisted medical methodology}}
'''Ambulatory assessment''' ('''AA''') is [[computer-assisted]] methodology for self-reports, behavior records or psychological measurements, while the subject undergoes normal activities in daily life.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Timmons |first1=Adela C. |last2=Baucom |first2=Brian R. |last3=Han |first3=Sohyun C. |last4=Perrone |first4=Laura |last5=Chaspari |first5=Theodora |last6=Narayanan |first6=Shrikanth S. |last7=Margolin |first7=Gayla |date=2017-06-15 |title=New Frontiers in Ambulatory Assessment |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1177/1948550617709115 |journal=Social Psychological and Personality Science |volume=8 |issue=5 |pages=552–563 |doi=10.1177/1948550617709115 |issn=1948-5506|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Weiner 2010">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=be0VYic5iWwC&dq=ambulatory+assessment+psychology&pg=PA76|title=The Corsini Encyclopedia of Psychology|last1=Weiner|first1=Irving B.|last2=Craighead|first2=W. Edward|date=2010-01-19|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=9780470170250|language=en}}</ref>

AA is used in clinical psychology to investigate symptoms, predict the recurrence or onset of new symptoms, monitor treatment effects, prevent relapse, and indicate necessary interventions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Trull |first1=Timothy J. |last2=Ebner-Priemer |first2=Ulrich |date=2013-03-28 |title=Ambulatory Assessment |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1146/annurev-clinpsy-050212-185510 |journal=Annual Review of Clinical Psychology |volume=9 |issue=1 |pages=151–176 |doi=10.1146/annurev-clinpsy-050212-185510 |pmid=23157450 |issn=1548-5943|pmc=4249763 }}</ref>

In the early ambulatory assessment, personal digital assistants and [[Interactive voice response|interactive voice response systems]] were used. They have now been replaced by [[smartphone]]s, and this has made [[data collection]] more feasible.<ref name="Trull 2013">{{Cite journal|last1=Trull|first1=Timothy J.|last2=Ebner-Priemer|first2=Ulrich|date=2013|title=Ambulatory Assessment |journal=[[Annual Review of Clinical Psychology]]|volume=9|pages=151–176|doi=10.1146/annurev-clinpsy-050212-185510 |pmc=4249763|pmid=23157450}}</ref>

== Characteristics ==
# The recording takes place in real-life situations
# A computer-assisted methodology is widely used
# The evaluator attempts to minimise the method dependent reactivity and strives to achieve a high degree of [[ecological balance]]<ref name="Weiner 2010" />
# The assessment can be continuous, event-based, interactive, time-based, or randomly prompted
# It is idiographic in focus and allows for the examination of multiple individual processes<ref name="Trull 2013" />

The Ambulatory assessment can be applied in various areas of [[psychology]] and other [[Behavioural sciences|behavioral sciences]].

== Modes of Data Collection ==

=== Event Controlled/Self-Report ===

The subject self-monitors the happenings of events and assess them whenever it occurs.<ref name="Weiner 2010" /> Varieties of devices are used to collect the data from the self reports.

The main concern with the self-report assessment is whether biases may influence the credibility of the results.<ref name="Trull 2013" />

=== Time Controlled/Observational ===

In this mode, the subject follows the time-sampling schedule.<ref name="Weiner 2010" /> This mode provides the data through the observer’s point of view. Forms of Ambulatory assessment observational method are Electronically Activated Recorder (EAR), [[Global Positioning System]] (GPS) in phones or devices on the person. Light sensors to infer context, using video or sensors to detect interactions with others.<ref name="Trull 2013" />
